title: Referrals and Prior Authorization Concepts

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the referral process from clinician order through specialist scheduling and closed-loop reporting.
- Explain prior authorization concepts, including medical necessity, coverage review, approvals, denials, and appeals.
- Recognize the documentation requirements for referrals, prior authorizations, and insurer and specialist communications.
- Apply scope-of-practice boundaries by gathering and relaying information and escalating clinical decisions to licensed staff.
- Communicate accurately and professionally with insurers, specialists, and patients throughout the referral and authorization processes.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A referral is like a teacher writing a note sending a student to a special tutor who can help with a specific subject.

### Question 2

The doctor is the one who decides a patient needs a specialist and writes the 'note' to go; the assistant helps make the appointment and send the papers.

### Question 3

If you have a problem with your eyes, your regular doctor sends you to an eye doctor who knows eyes best, instead of trying to fix it alone.

### Question 4

A referral is the doctor's note that says 'go see the heart doctor.' A prior authorization is the insurance company's green light that says 'yes, we will help pay for that heart visit.'

### Question 5

The assistant is like the helpful planner: once the doctor says 'see the skin doctor,' the assistant gathers the papers and helps get the appointment set up.

### Question 6

The referral form needs to say 'the patient has X problem, please check it out' so the specialist knows exactly what to look for.

### Question 7

A consultation is like asking a second teacher for their opinion and report; a referral is like sending the student to a different teacher to handle that subject for a while.

### Question 8

In-network doctors have a special deal with the insurance company, so visiting them usually costs the patient less money than going out-of-network.

### Question 9

Just like a library card needs your full name and card number to find your book, a referral needs correct patient details to find the right person and insurance.

### Question 10

The NPI is like a doctor's official ID number, so everyone knows exactly which doctor sent the patient.

### Question 11

You send only the pages the specialist needs to understand the problem, not the patient's whole file, and you make sure you have permission.

### Question 12

Think of medical records like a sealed report card: you need the right permission (and follow the office rules) before sharing it, even with another doctor.

### Question 13

A referral log is like a to-do list the whole office can see, so no referral gets forgotten.

### Question 14

If the specialist hasn't called, the assistant calls to make sure the papers arrived and the appointment is being set up.

### Question 15

Closing the loop is like making sure the teacher who sent the note gets the tutor's report back so everyone knows how the student is doing.

### Question 16

Urgent is like the 'priority' label on a package: it gets sent first and watched closely, not put at the bottom of the pile.

### Question 17

The assistant explains what will happen next and answers questions, like a friendly guide who shows the way without pretending to be the doctor.

### Question 18

The assistant is the connector who gathers the details, makes the calls, and tells the patient when and where to go.

### Question 19

An authorization number is like a receipt number for a special approval; you write it down so you can prove the approval happened.

### Question 20

Prior authorization is like asking a parent for permission before buying something expensive, so you know ahead of time whether it will be paid for.

### Question 21

It is like checking with the insurance company first to make sure a big, costly step is really needed and will be covered before you take it.

### Question 22

The doctor explains why the treatment is needed, and the assistant does the paperwork and phone calls to get it approved.

### Question 23

The doctor's note says 'go get the MRI,' but the insurance company still needs its own permission before it will pay.

### Question 24

Expensive or special things, like big scans, operations, special medicines, and equipment, are the ones the insurance company wants to approve first.

### Question 25

Medical necessity means the treatment is truly needed to help the patient's condition, not just wanted or expensive.

### Question 26

You need the full picture: who the patient is, what service is requested, why it is needed, and the proof to back it up.

### Question 27

Procedure codes are like a menu item number: they tell the insurance company exactly which service is being ordered.

### Question 28

The diagnosis code is like telling the insurance company 'this is what is wrong,' so it can decide if the treatment makes sense.

### Question 29

The insurance company needs the doctor's real notes and test results, like evidence, to see why the treatment is truly needed.

### Question 30

Sending the permission request early is like asking for a field-trip slip days before the trip, not the morning of.

### Question 31

When something can't wait, the assistant uses the insurance company's 'fast lane' and asks for help if it is stuck.

### Question 32

Retrospective means 'looking back': asking for approval after the care already happened because it could not be requested ahead of time.

### Question 33

When the insurance company says no, the assistant writes it down, tells the doctor, and finds out why and what can be done next.

### Question 34

The assistant helps put the appeal folder together and keeps track of it; the doctor explains the medical reasons.

### Question 35

Peer-to-peer is when the doctor who ordered the care talks directly with the insurance company's doctor to explain why it is needed.

### Question 36

A predetermination is like asking the insurance company for a price estimate before the work is done.

### Question 37

Before filling out the request, the assistant checks that the patient's insurance is active and that the plan actually covers the service.

### Question 38

First check the rules, gather the doctor's note and proof, send the request, then keep track of what happens.

### Question 39

The office can send the request through the insurance company's website, a secure fax, or a phone call that gets written down.

### Question 40

The assistant writes down the who, what, when, and how of the request, like keeping a careful diary entry.

### Question 41

The approval number goes in the patient's file, like filing an important receipt where you can find it later.

### Question 42

An approval is like a coupon with an expiration date; use it before it runs out, or ask for a new one.

### Question 43

If the approval covers six visits and the doctor wants more, the assistant asks the insurance company for more visits first.

### Question 44

Renewing is like getting a new library card when the old one expires, so the patient can keep using the service.

### Question 45

The assistant checks in with the insurance company now and then, writes down what was said, and asks for help if it is taking too long.

### Question 46

The assistant tells the patient what is happening and when the office will check again, without making promises no one can keep.

### Question 47

The assistant keeps the doctor in the loop because the doctor may need to add information or talk to the insurance company's doctor.

### Question 48

When the insurance says no to a medicine, the assistant writes it down and tells the doctor, who decides what to do next.

### Question 49

A tracking system is like a shared calendar of expiration dates so nothing important is forgotten.

### Question 50

The assistant writes down the important facts of the referral, like the who, why, and when.

### Question 51

The assistant writes a clear log of the request and its status, like keeping a receipt and notes for every step.

### Question 52

The assistant notes who they talked to, when, what was said, and any reference number, like taking minutes at a meeting.

### Question 53

A reference number is like a ticket number at a service desk, so you can pull up the exact conversation later.

### Question 54

The assistant writes a short note about what they told the patient, like jotting down a quick message to a teammate.

### Question 55

Good notes are like a paper trail that shows exactly what happened, so the whole team and the insurance company can see the truth.

### Question 56

The assistant writes down that the request was denied, when, why, and what the office did next.

### Question 57

The assistant records exactly when and how the appeal was sent and what is happening with it.

### Question 58

The assistant speaks politely, gives the correct facts, and writes down what was said, like a professional customer-service call.

### Question 59

The assistant shares the important details: who the patient is, which doctor sent them, why, and any approval number.

### Question 60

The packet is like a complete homework folder with the assignment (referral), the background (records), and the student ID (insurance).

### Question 61

The assistant calls to ask, 'Did you get our packet?' and writes down the answer.

### Question 62

If a piece is missing, the assistant gets the correct information from the doctor or the chart, instead of making something up.

### Question 63

The assistant tells the truth kindly, explains what the office is doing to fix it, and says when they will check again.

### Question 64

The report comes back to the doctor who sent the patient, gets put in the file, and the doctor reads it, closing the loop.

### Question 65

Each specialist gets only the folder for their own topic, and both reports come back to the main doctor, like two projects staying organized on one desk.

### Question 66

Using the insurance website is like tracking a package online: you can see where your request is at any time.

### Question 67

The assistant passes along the doctor's real reasons and asks the doctor when a medical question comes up.

### Question 68

When a question is for the doctor, the assistant politely says so and sets up a time for the doctor to answer.

### Question 69

The assistant reminds the patient that the doctor made the referral and suggests talking with the doctor about any worries.

### Question 70

The assistant is the organized helper who does the paperwork and phone calls so the doctor's plan can move forward.

### Question 71

If the insurance company questions the diagnosis, the assistant takes that question straight to the doctor.

### Question 72

Seeing a doctor outside the insurance company's list usually costs the patient more, so the assistant tells them before the appointment is booked.

### Question 73

The assistant helps the patient understand what their insurance covers and where to get a price idea, without making up a number.

### Question 74

Picking a doctor from the insurance company's list usually means the patient pays less, so the office looks for one when it can.

### Question 75

The office keeps the patient in the loop, like a coach updating the team so nobody is left wondering.

### Question 76

Getting the name and ID number right is like writing the correct address on an envelope, so the letter goes to the right house.

### Question 77

The assistant gives the referral one last careful look, like checking a test before turning it in.

### Question 78

Getting the green light means the insurance will help pay, but the patient may still have their usual share, like a ticket price.

### Question 79

Step therapy is like trying the basic option first; if it does not work, the fancier option can be approved.

### Question 80

The formulary is like the plan's menu of medicines it will help pay for.

### Question 81

For Medicare questions, the assistant looks at the official Medicare source and the patient's own plan details.

### Question 82

Starting the permission paperwork early leaves plenty of time, like turning in a big project well before the deadline.

### Question 83

Writing both dates is like checking that an appointment is inside the window the approval covers.

### Question 84

If you skip the permission step the plan required, the insurance may not pay, and someone could get stuck with the bill.

### Question 85

If the menu number doesn't match the order, the assistant checks and fixes it before sending, instead of guessing.
